question:
The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $050^\circ$.

Work out the bearing of $A$ from $B$.
hint: Going from $B$ back to $A$ is the exact opposite direction. Opposite directions differ by $180^\circ$.
solution:
The direction from $B$ to $A$ is opposite to the direction from $A$ to $B$, so the bearings differ by $180^\circ$.

$050^\circ$ is less than $180^\circ$, so add $180^\circ$:
$$050^\circ + 180^\circ = 230^\circ$$

question:
The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $130^\circ$.

Work out the bearing of $A$ from $B$.
solution:
What changed: the bearing is $130^\circ$ instead of $050^\circ$, but it is still less than $180^\circ$, so the rule is the same.
$$130^\circ + 180^\circ = 310^\circ$$

$B$ is south-east of $A$, so $A$ is north-west of $B$, which matches a bearing of about $310^\circ$.

question:
The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $230^\circ$.

Work out the bearing of $A$ from $B$.
hint: Adding $180^\circ$ would give more than $360^\circ$. What should you do instead?
solution:
What changed: the bearing is now more than $180^\circ$. Adding $180^\circ$ would give $410^\circ$, which is more than a full turn, so instead **subtract** $180^\circ$:
$$230^\circ - 180^\circ = 050^\circ$$

(This reverses the first question in the set, as it should: if $B$ is on $050^\circ$ from $A$, then $A$ is on $230^\circ$ from $B$, and vice versa.)

question:
Write each direction as a three-figure bearing.

**(a)** East
**(b)** South-west
**(c)** North-west
**(d)** $8^\circ$ east of north
hint: Start facing north ($000^\circ$) and turn clockwise. A quarter turn is $90^\circ$; south-west is halfway between south and west.
solution:
Measure clockwise from north and always write three digits.

**(a)** East is a quarter turn clockwise: $090^\circ$ (not $90^\circ$).

**(b)** South is $180^\circ$ and west is $270^\circ$; south-west is halfway: $225^\circ$.

**(c)** North-west is halfway between west ($270^\circ$) and north ($360^\circ$): $315^\circ$.

**(d)** $8^\circ$ clockwise from north: $008^\circ$. The leading zeros make it a three-figure bearing.

question:
The diagram shows the positions of three points $P$, $Q$ and $R$. (Not drawn to scale.)

**(a)** Work out the bearing of $Q$ from $P$.
**(b)** Work out the bearing of $R$ from $P$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 260" width="340" height="260"><line x1="170" y1="140" x2="170" y2="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M165 50 L170 40 L175 50" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="170" y="34" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">N</text><line x1="170" y1="140" x2="170" y2="235" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="170" y1="140" x2="109.8" y2="54" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="170" y1="140" x2="278.8" y2="190.7" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="170" cy="140" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="109.8" cy="54" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="278.8" cy="190.7" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><text x="182" y="144" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">P</text><text x="99.8" y="50" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">Q</text><text x="290.8" y="194.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">R</text><path d="M150.5 112.1 A34 34 0 0 1 170 106" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="155" y="97.3" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">35°</text><path d="M200.8 154.4 A34 34 0 0 1 170 174" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="197.9" y="188.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">65°</text></svg>
hint: Each bearing is the clockwise angle from the north line at $P$. For $R$ the $65^\circ$ is measured from south, which is $180^\circ$.
solution:
**(a)** $Q$ is $35^\circ$ to the **west** of north. Turning clockwise from north to face $Q$ is almost a full turn:
$$360^\circ - 35^\circ = 325^\circ$$

**(b)** Turning clockwise from north to south is $180^\circ$. $R$ is $65^\circ$ short of south (on the east side), so
$$180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$$

question:
The diagram shows a ship $S$ and a lighthouse $L$. (Not drawn to scale.)

Sophie says: "The angle between north and the line to the lighthouse is $25^\circ$, so the bearing of $L$ from $S$ is $025^\circ$."

Explain Sophie's mistake and give the correct bearing.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220"><line x1="180" y1="190" x2="180" y2="25" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M175 35 L180 25 L185 35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="180" y="19" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">N</text><line x1="180" y1="190" x2="116.6" y2="54.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="180" cy="190" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="116.6" cy="54.1" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><text x="190" y="206" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">S</text><text x="104.6" y="58.1" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">L</text><path d="M158.9 144.7 A50 50 0 0 1 180 140" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="165.3" y="128.6" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">25°</text></svg>
hint: Which way do bearings turn from north? Is $L$ to the east or to the west of the north line?
answer: She measured anticlockwise (the lighthouse is west of north). Correct bearing $= 335^\circ$.
solution:
**Mistake:** Bearings are always measured **clockwise** from north. $L$ is $25^\circ$ to the **west** of north, so the $25^\circ$ in the diagram is an anticlockwise angle. A bearing of $025^\circ$ would point $25^\circ$ east of north, on the other side of the north line.

**Correct bearing:** turning clockwise from north to face $L$:
$$360^\circ - 25^\circ = 335^\circ$$

question:
The bearing of $Q$ from $P$ is $048^\circ$. Tom is asked for the bearing of $P$ from $Q$. He writes:

"I draw the north line at $P$ and measure clockwise to $Q$. The angle is $48^\circ$, so the bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $048^\circ$."

Explain what Tom has done wrong and find the correct bearing.
hint: In "the bearing of $P$ from $Q$", which point do you stand at?
answer: He measured at the wrong point: the north line must be drawn at $Q$. Correct bearing $= 228^\circ$.
solution:
**Mistake:** "The bearing of $P$ **from** $Q$" means you stand at $Q$, draw the north line at $Q$, and turn clockwise until you face $P$. Tom drew the north line at $P$, so he found the bearing of $Q$ from $P$, which he was already given.

**Correct working:** facing from $Q$ to $P$ is the opposite direction to facing from $P$ to $Q$. $048^\circ < 180^\circ$, so
$$048^\circ + 180^\circ = 228^\circ$$

The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $228^\circ$.

question:
A boat sails from $A$ to $B$ on a bearing of $285^\circ$, then from $B$ to $C$ on a bearing of $160^\circ$. Ellie wants to find angle $ABC$. Her working is shown.

$$\text{Bearing of } A \text{ from } B = 285^\circ + 180^\circ = 465^\circ$$
$$\text{Angle } ABC = 465^\circ - 160^\circ = 305^\circ$$

**(a)** Explain the error in Ellie's first line.
**(b)** Find the correct size of angle $ABC$.
hint: A bearing must be less than $360^\circ$. When the bearing is $180^\circ$ or more, how do you find the back bearing?
answer: (a) $285^\circ \ge 180^\circ$, so she should subtract $180^\circ$; the back bearing is $105^\circ$. (b) $55^\circ$
solution:
**(a)** A bearing is always between $000^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. Ellie always added $180^\circ$; because $285^\circ$ is already more than $180^\circ$ she should **subtract** $180^\circ$:
$$\text{Bearing of } A \text{ from } B = 285^\circ - 180^\circ = 105^\circ$$

**(b)** At $B$, the direction to $A$ is $105^\circ$ and the direction to $C$ is $160^\circ$ (both clockwise from the same north line). The angle between them is
$$\text{Angle } ABC = 160^\circ - 105^\circ = 55^\circ$$

(Her answer of $305^\circ$ could not be an angle of a triangle anyway.)

question:
The diagram shows two points $A$ and $B$ with north lines drawn at each. The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $\theta$, where $0^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ$. (Not drawn to scale.)

**(a)** Explain why the angle marked $x$ is equal to $180^\circ - \theta$.
**(b)** Hence prove that the bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $\theta + 180^\circ$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 260" width="330" height="260"><line x1="80" y1="220" x2="80" y2="110" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M75 120 L80 110 L85 120" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="80" y="104" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">N</text><line x1="261.9" y1="115" x2="261.9" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M256.9 45 L261.9 35 L266.9 45" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="261.9" y="29" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">N</text><line x1="80" y1="220" x2="261.9" y2="115" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="80" cy="220" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="261.9" cy="115" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><text x="68" y="236" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="275.9" y="131" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><path d="M80 182 A38 38 0 0 1 112.9 201" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="107" y="178.2" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">θ</text><line x1="261.9" y1="115" x2="261.9" y2="175" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><path d="M235.9 130 A30 30 0 0 1 261.9 85" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="222" y="97" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x</text></svg>
hint: The two north lines are parallel. What do you know about co-interior angles between parallel lines?
answer: (a) The north lines are parallel and $AB$ is a transversal, so $\theta$ and $x$ are co-interior angles, which add to $180^\circ$. (b) Bearing of $A$ from $B$ $= 360^\circ - x = 360^\circ - (180^\circ - \theta) = 180^\circ + \theta$.
solution:
**(a)** All north lines point the same way, so the north lines at $A$ and $B$ are parallel. $AB$ crosses both of them. The angles $\theta$ (at $A$) and $x$ (at $B$) lie between the parallel lines on the same side of $AB$, so they are **co-interior** (allied) angles and add to $180^\circ$:
$$x = 180^\circ - \theta$$

**(b)** At $B$, the angle $x$ is measured **anticlockwise** from north round to $A$. The clockwise angle from north to $A$ (the bearing) is the rest of the full turn:
$$\text{bearing of } A \text{ from } B = 360^\circ - x = 360^\circ - (180^\circ - \theta) = \theta + 180^\circ$$

For example, if $\theta = 060^\circ$, the bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $240^\circ$.

question:
Kim says: "If the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is between $000^\circ$ and $090^\circ$, then the bearing of $A$ from $B$ must be between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$."

**(a)** Is Kim correct? Explain your answer.
**(b)** Raj is told that the bearing of $D$ from $C$ is $230^\circ$. He says the bearing of $C$ from $D$ is $410^\circ$. Explain why this cannot be a bearing, find the correct bearing, and show that your answer fits Kim's statement.
hint: Add $180^\circ$ to every bearing in the range $000^\circ$ to $090^\circ$. For (b), what range must every bearing lie in?
answer: (a) Yes: adding $180^\circ$ to a bearing between $000^\circ$ and $090^\circ$ gives one between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ (north-east becomes south-west). (b) Bearings are less than $360^\circ$; since $230^\circ \ge 180^\circ$ he should subtract: $050^\circ$. Then $C$ from $D$ is $050^\circ$ (between $000^\circ$ and $090^\circ$) and $D$ from $C$ is $230^\circ$ (between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$), as Kim says.
solution:
**(a)** If the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $\theta$ with $0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ$, then $\theta < 180^\circ$, so the back bearing is $\theta + 180^\circ$, and
$$180^\circ \le \theta + 180^\circ \le 270^\circ$$

Kim is correct. In words: if $B$ is somewhere north-east of $A$, then $A$ is somewhere south-west of $B$.

**(b)** A bearing is an amount of clockwise turn from north, so it is always at least $000^\circ$ and less than $360^\circ$; $410^\circ$ is more than a full turn. Raj always added $180^\circ$, but $230^\circ \ge 180^\circ$, so he should have subtracted:
$$230^\circ - 180^\circ = 050^\circ$$

(Equivalently $410^\circ - 360^\circ = 050^\circ$.) So the bearing of $C$ from $D$ is $050^\circ$, which is between $000^\circ$ and $090^\circ$, and the bearing of $D$ from $C$ is $230^\circ$, which is between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$. This is exactly Kim's statement with the roles of the points swapped.

question:
On a walking map with scale $1 : 50\,000$, a church $C$ is 6.4 cm from a school $S$. The bearing of the church from the school is $125^\circ$.

**(a)** Work out the real distance between the school and the church, in kilometres.
**(b)** Work out the bearing of the school from the church.
**(c)** A footbridge $F$ is 3.2 km due east of the school. On the map, how far is the footbridge from the school, in cm?
hint: 1 cm on the map represents $50\,000$ cm in real life. Convert to km: $100\,000$ cm $= 1$ km.
solution:
**(a)**
$$6.4 \times 50\,000 = 320\,000 \text{ cm} = 3200 \text{ m} = 3.2 \text{ km}$$

**(b)** Back bearing: $125^\circ < 180^\circ$, so add $180^\circ$:
$$125^\circ + 180^\circ = 305^\circ$$

**(c)** 3.2 km is the same real distance as in (a), so it is 6.4 cm on the map. (Check: $3.2 \text{ km} = 320\,000$ cm, and $320\,000 \div 50\,000 = 6.4$ cm.)

(On a scale drawing, $F$ would be drawn 6.4 cm from $S$ on a bearing of $090^\circ$, and $C$ 6.4 cm from $S$ on $125^\circ$.)

question:
A hiker walks 5 km due south from a car park $P$, then 12 km due west to a campsite $C$.

**(a)** How far is the campsite from the car park in a straight line?
**(b)** Work out the bearing of the campsite from the car park, to the nearest degree.
**(c)** Write down the bearing she should follow to walk straight back from the campsite to the car park.
hint: South then west makes a right angle. Find the angle at $P$ between the south direction and $PC$, then add it to $180^\circ$.
solution:
Let $T$ be the turning point. Triangle $PTC$ has a right angle at $T$, with $PT = 5$ km and $TC = 12$ km.

**(a)**
$$PC = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13 \text{ km}$$

**(b)** The angle at $P$ between south and $PC$:
$$\tan \angle TPC = \frac{12}{5} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \angle TPC = 67.38\ldots^\circ$$

Turning clockwise from north: $180^\circ$ to face south, then a further $67.38^\circ$ towards west:
$$180^\circ + 67.38^\circ = 247.38\ldots^\circ \approx 247^\circ$$

**(c)** $247.38^\circ \ge 180^\circ$, so subtract: $247.38^\circ - 180^\circ = 67.38^\circ$, i.e. $067^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

question: A buoy $B$ is 7 km from a harbour $H$ on a bearing of $040^\circ$. (Not drawn accurately.)
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 260" width="320" height="260"><line x1="100" y1="230" x2="100" y2="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M95 50 L100 40 L105 50" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="100" y="34" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">N</text><line x1="100" y1="230" x2="222.1" y2="84.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="100" cy="230" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="222.1" cy="84.5" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><text x="88" y="246" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">H</text><text x="236.1" y="88.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><path d="M100 184 A46 46 0 0 1 129.6 194.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="121.9" y="174.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">40°</text><text x="177.1" y="175.2" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">7 km</text></svg>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Work out how far north of $H$ the buoy is. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Work out how far east of $H$ the buoy is. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write down the bearing of $H$ from $B$.

hint: Draw a right-angled triangle with the 7 km line as the hypotenuse and the north line at $H$ as one side. The $40^\circ$ is at $H$.
solution:
Make a right-angled triangle: from $B$ draw a line due west to meet the north line at $H$, at point $X$. Then $HX$ is the distance north and $XB$ the distance east, with angle $XHB = 40^\circ$ and hypotenuse $HB = 7$ km.

**(a)**
$$HX = 7\cos 40^\circ \quad \text{M1}$$

$$= 5.362\ldots \approx 5.36 \text{ km} \quad \text{A1}$$

**(b)**
$$XB = 7\sin 40^\circ \quad \text{M1}$$

$$= 4.499\ldots \approx 4.50 \text{ km} \quad \text{A1}$$

**(c)** $040^\circ + 180^\circ = 220^\circ$ B1

question: A ship sails 12 km from port $P$ on a bearing of $070^\circ$ to a point $Q$. It then sails 15 km on a bearing of $190^\circ$ to a point $R$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Work out the distance $PR$. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Work out the bearing of $R$ from $P$. Give your answer to the nearest degree.

hint: Sketch it with a north line at $Q$. The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is the back bearing of $070^\circ$. Then the triangle is not right-angled, so use the cosine rule.
solution:
**(a)** Bearing of $P$ from $Q$ $= 070^\circ + 180^\circ = 250^\circ$ B1.

At $Q$ the direction to $R$ is $190^\circ$ and to $P$ is $250^\circ$, so
$$\angle PQR = 250^\circ - 190^\circ = 60^\circ \quad \text{B1 (shown)}$$

**(b)** Cosine rule:
$$PR^2 = 12^2 + 15^2 - 2 \times 12 \times 15 \times \cos 60^\circ \quad \text{M1}$$

$$PR^2 = 144 + 225 - 180 = 189 \quad \text{M1}$$

$$PR = \sqrt{189} = 13.74\ldots \approx 13.7 \text{ km} \quad \text{A1}$$

**(c)** Find angle $QPR$ (cosine rule avoids any ambiguity):
$$\cos \angle QPR = \frac{12^2 + 189 - 15^2}{2 \times 12 \times \sqrt{189}} = \frac{108}{24\sqrt{189}} = 0.3273\ldots \quad \text{M1}$$

$$\angle QPR = 70.89\ldots^\circ \quad \text{A1}$$

$R$ is clockwise from $Q$ as seen from $P$, so
$$\text{bearing} = 070^\circ + 70.89^\circ = 140.89^\circ \approx 141^\circ \quad \text{B1 ft}$$

question:
Two ships leave a port $O$ at 09:00. Ship $A$ sails at 18 km/h on a bearing of $025^\circ$. Ship $B$ sails at 24 km/h on a bearing of $115^\circ$.

**(a)** How far apart are the ships at 10:30?
**(b)** Work out the bearing of ship $B$ from ship $A$ at 10:30, to the nearest degree.
hint: Use distance $=$ speed $\times$ time for each ship. What is the angle between bearings $025^\circ$ and $115^\circ$?
solution:
Time taken: 09:00 to 10:30 is 1.5 hours.
$$OA = 18 \times 1.5 = 27 \text{ km}, \qquad OB = 24 \times 1.5 = 36 \text{ km}$$

The angle between the two courses is $115^\circ - 25^\circ = 90^\circ$, so angle $AOB$ is a right angle.

**(a)**
$$AB = \sqrt{27^2 + 36^2} = \sqrt{729 + 1296} = \sqrt{2025} = 45 \text{ km}$$

**(b)** In right-angled triangle $AOB$:
$$\tan \angle OAB = \frac{36}{27} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \angle OAB = 53.13\ldots^\circ$$

The bearing of $O$ from $A$ is the back bearing $025^\circ + 180^\circ = 205^\circ$. Facing $O$ from $A$ means facing south-west; ship $B$, which is south-east of $O$, is then on the left, so turn **anticlockwise** by $53.13^\circ$:
$$205^\circ - 53.13^\circ = 151.87^\circ \approx 152^\circ$$

Check with east/north coordinates (km): $A = (27\sin 25^\circ, 27\cos 25^\circ) = (11.41, 24.47)$, $B = (36\sin 115^\circ, 36\cos 115^\circ) = (32.63, -15.21)$. From $A$ to $B$: 21.22 km east and 39.68 km south, so the bearing is $180^\circ - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{21.22}{39.68}\right) = 180^\circ - 28.13^\circ = 151.87^\circ$. ✓

question:
A lighthouse $L$ is 8 km due east of a port $P$. A boat $B$ is on a bearing of $040^\circ$ from $P$ and on a bearing of $300^\circ$ from $L$. (Not drawn to scale.)

**(a)** Work out the three angles of triangle $PLB$.
**(b)** A student makes a scale drawing using 1 cm to represent 1 km. Describe how she would locate $B$.
**(c)** Calculate the distance of the boat from the port, to 3 significant figures.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 260" width="330" height="260"><line x1="50" y1="230" x2="50" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M45 90 L50 80 L55 90" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="50" y="74" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">N</text><line x1="290" y1="230" x2="290" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M285 90 L290 80 L295 90" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="290" y="74" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">N</text><line x1="50" y1="230" x2="290" y2="230" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="230" x2="128.3" y2="136.7" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="290" y1="230" x2="128.3" y2="136.7" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="50" cy="230" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="290" cy="230" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="128.3" cy="136.7" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><text x="38" y="246" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">P</text><text x="302" y="246" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">L</text><text x="128.3" y="126.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="170" y="250" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">8 km</text></svg>
hint: At $P$, the angle between north and $PB$ is $40^\circ$, and $PL$ points east ($090^\circ$). At $L$, the direction to $P$ is $270^\circ$.
answer: (a) $\angle P = 50^\circ$, $\angle L = 30^\circ$, $\angle B = 100^\circ$ (b) Draw $PL = 8$ cm; draw a line from $P$ on $040^\circ$ and from $L$ on $300^\circ$; $B$ is where they cross. (c) 4.06 km
solution:
**(a)** At $P$: $PL$ is on bearing $090^\circ$ and $PB$ on $040^\circ$, so $\angle LPB = 90^\circ - 40^\circ = 50^\circ$.

At $L$: $LP$ is on bearing $270^\circ$ and $LB$ on $300^\circ$, so $\angle PLB = 300^\circ - 270^\circ = 30^\circ$.

$\angle PBL = 180^\circ - 50^\circ - 30^\circ = 100^\circ$.

**(b)** Draw $P$ and $L$ 8 cm apart with $L$ due east of $P$. Draw north lines at both. At $P$ measure $40^\circ$ clockwise from north and draw a long line; at $L$ measure $300^\circ$ clockwise from north (i.e. $60^\circ$ anticlockwise) and draw a long line. $B$ is where the lines cross; measure $PB$ in cm and convert to km.

**(c)** Sine rule: $PB$ is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle and $PL = 8$ is opposite the $100^\circ$ angle:
$$\frac{PB}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{8}{\sin 100^\circ}$$

$$PB = \frac{8\sin 30^\circ}{\sin 100^\circ} = \frac{4}{0.9848\ldots} = 4.061\ldots \approx 4.06 \text{ km}$$

(A careful scale drawing should give about 4.1 cm.)

question:
**Do not use a calculator.** A drone flies 10 km from $A$ on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to $B$. It then flies 10 km on a bearing of $270^\circ$ to $C$.

Without using trigonometry, find the distance and the bearing of $C$ from $A$. Explain your reasoning fully.
hint: Work out angle $ABC$ using the back bearing of $150^\circ$. What kind of triangle has two equal sides and that angle between them?
solution:
**Angle at $B$.** The bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $150^\circ + 180^\circ = 330^\circ$. The bearing of $C$ from $B$ is $270^\circ$. So
$$\angle ABC = 330^\circ - 270^\circ = 60^\circ$$

**Shape of the triangle.** $AB = BC = 10$ km, so triangle $ABC$ is isosceles, and the base angles are $\frac{180^\circ - 60^\circ}{2} = 60^\circ$ each. All three angles are $60^\circ$, so the triangle is **equilateral** and $AC = 10$ km.

**Bearing.** At $A$, angle $BAC = 60^\circ$. $C$ is reached by flying due west from $B$, so from $A$ the direction to $C$ is $60^\circ$ further round towards the west than the direction to $B$. Turning clockwise from $150^\circ$ goes towards south ($180^\circ$) and then west, so
$$\text{bearing of } C \text{ from } A = 150^\circ + 60^\circ = 210^\circ$$

Check: $C$ is 10 km from $A$ on $210^\circ$ ($30^\circ$ west of south) and $B$ is 10 km from $A$ on $150^\circ$ ($30^\circ$ east of south). These are mirror images in the south line, so $B$ is due east of $C$ and the last leg $B \to C$ is indeed on $270^\circ$. ✓

question:
A rock $R$ is 6 km due north of a coastguard station $C$. A boat $B$ is on a bearing of $050^\circ$ from $C$, and is 5 km from the rock.

**(a)** Show that there are two possible positions for the boat, and find the distance $CB$ for each, to 3 significant figures.
**(b)** For the position of the boat that is further from $C$, find the bearing of the boat from the rock, to the nearest degree.
hint: In triangle $CRB$ you know $CR = 6$, $RB = 5$ and the angle at $C$ (between north and $CB$). Use the sine rule to find angle $CBR$ and remember the obtuse possibility.
solution:
**(a)** In triangle $CRB$: $CR = 6$ km, $RB = 5$ km, and the angle at $C$ between north ($CR$) and $CB$ is $50^\circ$. $RB = 5$ is opposite angle $C$, $CR = 6$ is opposite angle $B$:
$$\frac{\sin B}{6} = \frac{\sin 50^\circ}{5} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \sin B = \frac{6\sin 50^\circ}{5} = 0.9192\ldots$$

$$B = 66.82^\circ \quad \text{or} \quad B = 180^\circ - 66.82^\circ = 113.18^\circ$$

Both are valid: $50^\circ + 66.82^\circ < 180^\circ$ and $50^\circ + 113.18^\circ < 180^\circ$. (The known angle is opposite the shorter given side, $5 < 6$, and $5 > 6\sin 50^\circ = 4.60$, so the circle of radius 5 km round the rock cuts the $050^\circ$ line twice.)

* $B = 66.82^\circ$: angle $R = 180^\circ - 50^\circ - 66.82^\circ = 63.18^\circ$, and $CB = \dfrac{5\sin 63.18^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} = 5.83$ km.
* $B = 113.18^\circ$: angle $R = 16.82^\circ$, and $CB = \dfrac{5\sin 16.82^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} = 1.89$ km.

**(b)** The further position has $\angle CRB = 63.18^\circ$. At $R$, the direction to $C$ is due south ($180^\circ$), and the boat is east of the line $RC$, so turning from south back towards east (anticlockwise) by $63.18^\circ$:
$$\text{bearing of } B \text{ from } R = 180^\circ - 63.18^\circ = 116.82^\circ \approx 117^\circ$$
